title: The Prime 2: Order of 1 + 2·a and the Non-Cyclicity of (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ
description: Pins down how the prime 2 breaks the odd-prime pattern for unit groups of prime-power moduli. For odd p, every 1 + p·a (p ∤ a) attains the maximal p-power order p^(k-1) and (ℤ/pᵏℤ)ˣ is cyclic; at p = 2 both fail. The clean order formula is carried by 1 + 4·a (a odd), giving order 2^(k-2) — not by all of 1 + 2·a, since 1 + 2·a with a odd lies in the ≡ 3 mod 4 coset. As a consequence (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ is non-cyclic for k ≥ 3, proved here constructively by exhibiting two distinct involutions −1 and 1 + 2^(k-1) and counting order-2 elements via φ(2) = 1 — a more elementary architecture than Mathlib's reduction through (ℤ/8ℤ)ˣ. Fully verified: 0 axioms, 0 sorries, no native_decide.

Honest framing of the open question: for p = 2 the clean order formula is carried by 1 + 4·a (a odd), not 1 + 2·a — the residue of 1 + 2·a mod 4 already splits the units into two cosets, only one of which (≡ 1 mod 4) attains the maximal 2-power order 2^(k-2). This is the precise sense in which '1 + 2·a behaves differently' from the odd-prime case.

overview.historicalContext: Gauss showed that (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ is cyclic — i.e. a primitive root exists — exactly for n = 1, 2, 4, pᵏ, and 2pᵏ with p an odd prime. The exceptional case is the prime 2: (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ is cyclic only for k ≤ 2, and for k ≥ 3 it splits as ℤ/2 × ℤ/2^(k-2), the smallest instance being (ℤ/8ℤ)ˣ ≅ Klein four. The classical obstruction is that 8 has more than one square root of 1: alongside ±1 there is 1 + 2^(k-1). This entry, a p = 2 companion to the odd-prime order computation 1 + p·a, formalises both halves of the anomaly — the order formula and the non-cyclicity — with an explicit constructive witness.
overview.problemStatement: For the prime 2, determine the multiplicative order of elements 1 + 2·a modulo 2ᵏ and the cyclicity of (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ, contrasting with the odd-prime case where 1 + p·a (p ∤ a) has order p^(k-1) and the unit group is cyclic.
overview.proofStrategy: Two parts. (1) Record the corrected order formula orderOf(1 + 4·a) = 2^(k-2) for odd a (the factor is 4, not 2, since 1 + 2·a with a odd sits in the ≡ 3 mod 4 coset), with 5 = 1 + 4 the textbook generator. (2) Prove (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ non-cyclic for k ≥ 3 constructively: a finite cyclic group has exactly φ(2) = 1 element of order 2, but the unit group has two — −1 (order 2 since the ring has characteristic 2ᵏ ≠ 2) and the special involution 1 + 2^(k-1) (whose square is 1 + 2ᵏ + 2^(2k-2) ≡ 1, established by a ℕ-level ModEq congruence). These are distinct exactly for k ≥ 3, so counting involutions via IsCyclic.card_orderOf_eq_totient yields a contradiction.
keyInsights: **The factor 4, not 2, carries the maximal order.** Unlike the odd-prime case where every 1 + p·a works, at p = 2 only the principal units 1 + 4ℤ (generated by 5) attain order 2^(k-2); 1 + 2·a with a odd lands in the −1 coset (≡ 3 mod 4) and does not generate the maximal cyclic 2-group.

**Non-cyclicity is witnessed by a named pair of involutions.** −1 and 1 + 2^(k-1) are two distinct elements of order 2, whereas a cyclic group has exactly φ(2) = 1. This is a fully constructive obstruction, contrasting Mathlib's reduction-through-(ℤ/8ℤ)ˣ proof.

**The special involution squares to 1 by a clean 2-adic identity.** (1 + 2^(k-1))² = 1 + 2ᵏ + 2^(2k-2), and both added terms vanish mod 2ᵏ — proved through a natural-number ModEq congruence, keeping the argument axiom-free.

**This isolates 2ᵏ (k ≥ 3) as the unique non-cyclic prime-power modulus.** Once the odd-prime case is known cyclic, the cyclicity dichotomy (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ cyclic ⟺ k ≤ 2 pins the failure of primitive roots entirely to the high powers of two.

crossReferences.description: Parent: the odd-prime order computation orderOf(1 + p·a) = p^(k-1). This entry is the p = 2 companion, showing the formula needs the 1 + 4·a form and that the unit group fails to be cyclic for k ≥ 3.

Sibling computing the Carmichael function λ(2ᵏ) = 2^(k-2) and the absence of a primitive root mod 2ᵏ for k ≥ 3 — the same non-cyclicity of (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ, established there via the structure ℤ/2 × ℤ/2^(k-2) and here via an explicit two-involution witness.

conclusion.summary: At the prime 2 the structure of (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ departs from the odd-prime case in two linked ways. First, the maximal 2-power order is no longer carried by every 1 + 2·a: the clean order formula orderOf(1 + 4·a) = 2^(k-2) (a odd) needs the 1 + 4·a form, because the residue of 1 + 2·a modulo 4 already splits the units into the squares (≡ 1 mod 4) and the −1 coset (≡ 3 mod 4). Second, and as a consequence, the unit group is not cyclic for k ≥ 3: it carries two distinct involutions, −1 and 1 + 2^(k-1), whereas a cyclic group has exactly one. The file proves the non-cyclicity by exhibiting these two order-2 elements and counting involutions via φ(2) = 1.
implications: Isolates the prime 2 (powers ≥ 3) as the unique prime-power modulus whose unit group fails to be cyclic, complementing the parent's odd-prime order computation.
Gives a fully constructive obstruction to cyclicity — a named pair of involutions — rather than an abstract reduction, making the failure of cyclicity transparent.
Locates the maximal cyclic subgroup ⟨5⟩ of order 2^(k-2) inside (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ, the 2-adic analogue of the principal units 1 + pℤ for odd p.
openQuestions: Can one package the full isomorphism (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ ≃ ℤ/2 × ℤ/2^(k-2) for k ≥ 3, with explicit generators −1 and 5, mirroring the odd-prime isomorphism (ℤ/pᵏℤ)ˣ ≃ ℤ/p^(k-1) × ℤ/(p-1)?
What is the exact multiplicative order of a general 1 + 2·a modulo 2^k as a function of the 2-adic valuation v₂(a) and v₂(a+1), uniformly covering both the ⟨5⟩ coset and the −1 coset?
